paragraphs.heading: What friction is
paragraphs.text: Friction is the force that resists things sliding or grinding against each other, whether solid surfaces, layers of a fluid, or bits of material. It comes in several kinds, including dry, fluid, lubricated, skin and internal friction, and that list is not complete. The study of friction and related processes is called tribology. People have been studying it for more than 2,000 years.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: Friction can have dramatic results: rubbing two pieces of wood together can start a fire. It also causes wear, which can make machines work worse or damage their parts. Losses of energy to friction make up about 20% of all the energy the world uses.

paragraphs.heading: Where the energy goes
paragraphs.text: Many things add to the drag of friction. They range from the squashing of asperities, which are features of a surface, to the creation of charges and changes in the material's structure. As two touching bodies move past each other, some of their mechanical energy turns into heat and other losses. The friction force equals the energy lost for each unit of distance moved, written F=E/d. Because so much is going on, friction is hard to work out from first principles, so it is often studied by measurement instead.

paragraphs.heading: The main kinds
paragraphs.text: Dry friction resists two solid surfaces in contact moving sideways past each other. It splits into static friction, sometimes called stiction, between surfaces that are not moving, and kinetic friction between surfaces that are. Fluid friction acts between layers of a viscous fluid moving relative to each other, and lubricated friction is the case where a fluid keeps two solid surfaces apart. Skin friction is part of drag, the force that resists a fluid flowing across a body. Internal friction resists the parts of a solid moving against each other as it changes shape.

paragraphs.heading: Early discoveries
paragraphs.text: Ancient writers including Aristotle, Vitruvius and Pliny the Elder wondered what causes friction and how to reduce it. They knew that keeping a moving thing moving is easier than getting a resting thing started, as Themistius noted in 350 A.D. Leonardo da Vinci found the classic laws of sliding friction in 1493, but his notebooks went unpublished and the laws stayed unknown. Guillaume Amontons found them again in 1699, and they became known as Amontons' three laws of dry friction. In 1785 Charles-Augustin de Coulomb tested how friction depends on the materials and their coatings, the area of contact, the load pressing down, and how long the surfaces had rested together.

paragraphs.heading: Friction makes heat
paragraphs.text: As scientists worked out the conservation of energy and the first law of thermodynamics, friction came to be seen as a way of turning mechanical work into heat. In 1798 Benjamin Thompson reported on experiments boring cannons. In 1842 Julius Robert Mayer warmed paper pulp by friction and measured how much its temperature rose. In 1845 Joule published a paper, The Mechanical Equivalent of Heat, giving a number for the work needed to make a unit of heat. One of his methods used a paddle wheel turning in a tub of water.
